chapter_theme: Coveting another's goods destroys one even in the wanting. Not wanting is presented as the real security of wealth, and it ends as a kind of pride and victory.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the faults of coveting (171-177), the good of not coveting (178-179), and both together (180). Many verses play on the sound of வெஃகு against அஃகு, to covet against to shrink.

171.reading: If one covets another's good things and leaves aside fairness, the family perishes, and faults come at once.
171.nuance: The condition is only வெஃகின், if one covets, and ஆங்கே, right then, makes the penalty immediate. Parimelazhagar gives நடுவு a specific meaning: the recognition that what belongs to others isn't ours to take.

172.reading: Those ashamed of unfairness won't do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had.
172.nuance: நாணு, shame, is the operative word and it means this person is restrained from inside. Parimelazhagar glosses it with fear, which is a less interior motive than the verse's word.

173.reading: Those who want the other joy won't do what's contrary to virtue out of desire for a small joy.
173.nuance: சிற்றின்பம் here refers to pleasure from taking others' goods, which isn't its common later meaning of sexual pleasure. The verse leaves 'the other joy' unnamed.

positions.position: The other joy is the lasting joy that comes from virtue.
The other joy is the great joy of release.
It's a lasting benefit that one wants in place of an immediate one.

174.reading: Those of faultless sight, who have conquered the senses, won't covet at the thought 'we have nothing'.
174.nuance: Need is the hardest case, and the verse rules out that excuse. Parimelazhagar goes a step further and says that such people don't count as poor at all, which removes the case instead of answering it.

175.reading: What is the use of fine and wide understanding if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone?
175.nuance: The sound of அஃகி, to be fine, is played against வெஃகி, to covet, and a learned mind is shown undone by the same sound. Parimelazhagar repeats a principle from 140: the purpose of understanding is what one refrains from.

176.reading: One standing on the path out of desire for grace will perish if, desiring wealth, he plots wrongs.
176.nuance: வெஃகி is used twice: he desires grace and he desires wealth, in the one verb. The other notable word is சூழ, to plot: Parimelazhagar notes that it says the plotting alone destroys him, let alone the doing.

positions.position: The path is household life, called a path because one can't renounce until understanding matures in it.
positions.quote: இல்லற நெறியில் அறிவு முதிர்ந்துழி அல்லது துறக்கப் படாமையின், அதனைத் துறவறத்திற்கு 'ஆறு' என்றார்.

positions.position: The path is simply the way of virtue, and even one with grace can fall.

177.reading: Don't seek gain that comes by coveting: when it ripens, its fruit is hard to make good.
177.nuance: The word விளைவயின் brings in a harvest image: the wrong shows only when the crop comes in, so the problem is one of delayed consequences.

178.reading: What keeps wealth from shrinking? Not coveting what's in another's hand, which that person wants.
178.nuance: The chapter's sound play, அஃகாமை and வெஃகாமை, is itself the answer. It offers a security for wealth that the wealthy might not expect: leaving others' goods alone.

179.reading: Fortune, knowing the way to come, approaches those who understand virtue and do not covet.
179.nuance: Here the goddess has to work out the right way to approach, as if she were the supplicant. Parimelazhagar's gloss explains the 'way' as time, place and the right moment.

180.reading: Coveting without thought yields destruction, and the pride called not-wanting yields victory.
180.nuance: செருக்கு normally means arrogance, and here it's a virtue. Parimelazhagar explains why it's a victory: it puts beneath it all those who scramble after wealth. Not wanting is a form of power.

links.note: In 39, joy comes only from virtue. Here that claim is put to work: the 'small joy' of taking others' goods is set against a greater one, and on Parimelazhagar's reading, the greater is the same joy of virtue as 39.

In 46 there's nothing to gain by leaving household life. Parimelazhagar on 176 calls household life a path toward renunciation, so leaving is the natural end. This commentator's way of ordering the stages conflicts with the plain force of 46.
Both promise that wealth lasts on a moral condition: fairness in 112 and not coveting in 178. The second is the first's inward side, since 171 treats coveting as itself a lapse from fairness.

Virtue in 130 and fortune in 179 both seek out the right person, and they look for the right moment to do so. Parimelazhagar uses செவ்வி in both notes. Moral power is pictured as a courtier waiting for an opening.
Not wanting yields victory here, and in 363 it's the choicest wealth in this world and the next. Chapter 18 is about not wanting others' goods, and 363 extends this to not wanting at all.

source_issues: Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 175. His entry for verse 177 opens with a fragment of the verse.
